stages.name: Reconnaissance
stages.description: Target selection, public exposure, asset discovery, and the intelligence that makes an intrusion possible.
stages.defense: Review exposed services and public information; distinguish external reconnaissance from discovery after access.

stages.name: Weaponization
stages.description: Payloads, exploits, malicious documents, and compromised build artifacts prepared for an operation.
stages.defense: Study payload structure and provenance. Static capability clues support hypotheses; they do not prove execution.

stages.name: Delivery
stages.description: Email, web content, removable media, software updates, and other routes that bring an adversary-controlled artifact to a target.
stages.defense: Correlate email, browser, download, and endpoint evidence to establish how an artifact arrived.

stages.name: Exploitation
stages.description: Vulnerability exploitation, user execution, and trust or credential abuse that turn exposure into access.
stages.defense: Connect the triggering request or action to execution and identity evidence. Credential abuse is not automatically a software exploit.

stages.name: Installation
stages.description: Deployment of implants, backdoors, malicious components, or mechanisms that maintain access.
stages.defense: Examine file, process, service, task, and configuration changes. Persistence can support installation, but the two are not synonyms.

stages.name: Command and Control
stages.description: Channels through which an operator or infrastructure communicates with compromised systems.
stages.defense: Combine DNS, HTTP/TLS, flow metadata, and endpoint context. A suspicious connection alone does not establish C2.

stages.name: Actions on Objectives
stages.description: Theft, espionage, disruption, destruction, encryption, fraud, and other mission outcomes.
stages.defense: Relate collection, movement, and impact evidence to the objective; distinguish demonstrated harm from plausible capability.
